summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, that lets the two ends of a connection negotiate vertical tab stops for output, meaning the lines on a page where a vertical tab should land. It is a companion to the horizontal tab options by the same author. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Besides jumping sideways, old printers could jump down the page to set lines. This note lets two computers agree on which lines those are.

subtitle: Negotiating vertical tab stops on a Telnet connection.

tldr.problem: When a remote system sends text over Telnet with vertical tab characters, the two sides need to agree on where the vertical tab stops are (the line numbers where a vertical tab should land on a page).
tldr.mechanism: This option defines commands that let the sender and receiver negotiate who should handle vertical tabs and what the stop line numbers should be. They exchange messages with stop values and reach agreement, paralleling the horizontal tabstops option (RFC 653).
tldr.outcome: Both sides know which party controls vertical tabs and where they are set. The RFC is Historic and no longer used in modern systems.

today: RFC 656 is Historic and has not been updated. The option is no longer used in practice; modern terminal applications do not typically support vertical tab stops at all.

sections.title: The Telnet Vertical Tab Stop Negotiation Option
sections.content: RFC 656 defines the NAOVTS option (Negotiate About Output Vertical Tabstops), a Telnet option for handling vertical tab stops in output. While RFC 653 dealt with horizontal positioning (columns), this RFC covers vertical positioning (lines on a page). A vertical tab character (ASCII 11) tells a printer or terminal to advance to the next vertical tab stop—a marked line number on the page. Both sides need to know where these stops are to align output correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Printers could jump down to set lines, like a ruler marked in rows. This option lets two computers agree on which lines those are.

sections.title: How Vertical Tab Stops Are Negotiated
sections.content:
The negotiation follows the same pattern as RFC 653. One side sends IAC DO NAOVTS and the other replies with IAC WILL NAOVTS or IAC WON'T NAOVTS. After agreement, the sides use subnegotiation messages. A value of zero means the sender will handle vertical tabs. Values 1 to 250 specify vertical tab stop line numbers (relative to the top of the page or terminal screen). Values 251 to 254 are not allowed (reserved for compatibility). A value of 255 means the receiver should handle it and decide the stops itself.

The rule is the same as before: if both sides want to handle vertical tabs, the sender wins. If neither wants to, the receiver must.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers negotiate with standard Telnet commands. Then they exchange line numbers where tabs should stop. The sender wins if both want control; otherwise the receiver handles it.

sections.title: Using Vertical Tab Stops
sections.content: Once negotiated, when a vertical tab character arrives, the receiver knows which party controls it and where the stops are set. The receiver applies the vertical tab by advancing the cursor down the page to the next marked line number. The data sender uses code DS (1) and the receiver uses code DR (0) to propose stop positions during subnegotiation. Either party can renegotiate at any time if circumstances change, such as when a new process starts or terminal settings shift.
sections.plainLanguage: After agreement, when a vertical tab arrives, the receiver jumps the cursor down to the next marked line. Either side can renegotiate the stops later if needed.
